## Proof

We evaluate the Riemann–Stieltjes integral $\int_0^1 f(x')\,dc(x')$ with $f(x)=1$ and $c$ the Cantor function.

**Key fact (Riemann–Stieltjes integral of a constant).** For any integrator $g$ of bounded variation on $[a,b]$ and any constant $f(x)=K$, the Riemann–Stieltjes integral exists and equals
$$\int_a^b K\,dg = K\bigl(g(b)-g(a)\bigr).$$

*Proof of the key fact.* For an arbitrary partition $P=\{a=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_n=b\}$ and any choice of sample points $\xi_i\in[x_{i-1},x_i]$, the Riemann–Stieltjes sum is
$$S(P,f,g)=\sum_{i=1}^{n} f(\xi_i)\bigl(g(x_i)-g(x_{i-1})\bigr)=K\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(g(x_i)-g(x_{i-1})\bigr).$$
The sum telescopes:
$$S(P,f,g)=K\bigl(g(x_n)-g(x_0)\bigr)=K\bigl(g(b)-g(a)\bigr).$$
Since every Riemann–Stieltjes sum equals the same value $K(g(b)-g(a))$ regardless of the partition or sample points, the integral exists and
$$\int_a^b K\,dg = K\bigl(g(b)-g(a)\bigr).$$

**Applying to our problem.** The Cantor function $c:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ is continuous and monotone non-decreasing, hence of bounded variation. With $K=1$, $a=0$, $b=1$:
$$\int_0^1 1\,dc(x') = 1\cdot\bigl(c(1)-c(0)\bigr).$$

The Cantor function satisfies $c(0)=0$ and $c(1)=1$ (it maps $[0,1]$ onto $[0,1]$, with $c=0$ on a neighborhood of $0$ and $c=1$ on a neighborhood of $1$). Therefore
$$\int_0^1 f(x')\,dc(x') = c(1)-c(0) = 1 - 0 = \boxed{1}.$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
